title: Blockchain Cryptography Puzzle Set
description: Ten puzzles covering foundational blockchain cryptography: SHA-256 hashing, Ed25519 signatures, public/private key operations, and Merkle tree construction and proofs.
author: Dujunior

puzzles.title: SHA-256 Single Block
puzzles.description: Compute the SHA-256 hash of the string `hello` and express it as a lowercase hex string.
hints: SHA-256 always produces a 256-bit (32-byte) output, represented as 64 hex characters.
The input is the UTF-8 encoding of the ASCII string `hello` with no newline.
puzzles.explanation: SHA-256 is a cryptographic hash function that maps any input to a fixed 256-bit digest. `hello` → `2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824`.

puzzles.title: SHA-256 Chained Hashing
puzzles.description: What is `SHA-256(SHA-256('blockchain'))`? First hash `blockchain`, then hash the hex-string result.
hints: Hash `blockchain` once to get a 64-character hex string.
Then treat that hex string as the literal ASCII input for the second SHA-256 call.
puzzles.explanation: Double-SHA-256 is used in Bitcoin's proof-of-work and transaction IDs. It provides extra preimage resistance over a single hash.

puzzles.title: Hash Collision Resistance
puzzles.description: Given two SHA-256 digests, determine whether they could have been produced by the same input. Explain why or why not, and state the probability of a random collision.
hints: SHA-256 is a deterministic function: the same input always produces the same output.
The probability of two random inputs sharing a hash is approximately 1/2^256.
puzzles.explanation: SHA-256 is collision-resistant: no two distinct inputs are known to produce the same digest. The birthday bound places the collision probability at around 1/2^128 for a random pair after 2^128 evaluations.

puzzles.title: Ed25519 Key Pair Generation
puzzles.description: Given a 32-byte secret seed `0x` + 64 hex chars, derive the corresponding Ed25519 public key. Express the public key as a 64-character lowercase hex string.
hints: Ed25519 uses the twisted Edwards curve over GF(2^255 - 19).
The public key is the compressed Y-coordinate of the base-point scalar multiple: `public_key = seed * G`.
Use a standard library such as `@noble/ed25519` (JavaScript) or Python's `cryptography` package.
puzzles.explanation: Stellar uses Ed25519 key pairs. The secret seed is encoded in base32 (Stellar strkey), but under the hood it is a 32-byte scalar used to derive the public key point on the Edwards curve.

puzzles.title: Ed25519 Message Signing
puzzles.description: Sign the UTF-8 message `StellarHunts` using the Ed25519 private key given as a 64-byte hex string (seed || public_key). Return the 64-byte signature as a lowercase hex string.
hints: Ed25519 signatures are deterministic — the same key and message always produce the same signature.
The 64-byte private key is the concatenation of the 32-byte seed and the 32-byte public key.
Use `nacl.sign.detached(message, secretKey)` (tweetnacl) or `ed25519.sign(message, privateKey)` (@noble/ed25519).
puzzles.explanation: Stellar transactions are signed with Ed25519. The signature covers the transaction hash, which is then verified on-chain using the account's registered public key.

puzzles.title: Ed25519 Signature Verification
puzzles.description: Given a public key, a message, and a signature (all as hex strings), determine whether the signature is valid. Output `true` or `false`.
hints: Ed25519 verification checks that `signature == sign(message, derive_private(seed))` without needing the private key.
A single flipped bit in the signature or message will produce `false`.
puzzles.explanation: Verification is the on-chain operation Stellar performs for every transaction. The validator calls `ed25519_verify(public_key, tx_hash, signature)` and rejects the transaction if it returns false.

puzzles.title: Public/Private Key Derivation Path
puzzles.description: Given a BIP-39 mnemonic and the Stellar derivation path `m/44'/148'/0'`, derive the Ed25519 key pair. Return the Stellar account ID (G... address) for the derived public key.
hints: Stellar uses SLIP-0010 for Ed25519 HD key derivation, not BIP-32.
The path `m/44'/148'/0'` corresponds to coin type 148 (Stellar) in SLIP-44.
Use `stellar-sdk`'s `Keypair.fromRawEd25519Seed()` after deriving the seed from the path.
puzzles.explanation: Stellar Lumens (XLM) uses coin type 148 in SLIP-44. The derivation follows SLIP-0010 because BIP-32 is only defined for secp256k1; Ed25519 requires the SLIP-0010 variant with hardened-only child keys.

puzzles.title: Merkle Tree Construction
puzzles.description: Given the leaf values `['tx1', 'tx2', 'tx3', 'tx4']`, build a SHA-256 Merkle tree and return the root hash as a lowercase hex string.
hints: Hash each leaf with SHA-256 to get the leaf nodes: `leaf_hash = SHA-256(leaf_value)`.
Pair adjacent nodes and hash their concatenation: `parent = SHA-256(left || right)`.
If there is an odd number of nodes at a level, duplicate the last node before pairing.
puzzles.explanation: Merkle trees allow efficient and tamper-evident proof that any element belongs to a dataset without transmitting the full dataset. Bitcoin block headers contain the Merkle root of all transactions in the block.

puzzles.title: Merkle Inclusion Proof
puzzles.description: Given a Merkle root, a leaf value, and an audit path (list of sibling hashes), verify that the leaf is included in the tree. Output `true` or `false`.
hints: Walk the audit path from the leaf to the root, hashing the current node with its sibling at each step.
The position bit in the proof indicates whether the sibling is on the left or right.
If your computed root matches the given root, the proof is valid.
puzzles.explanation: Merkle proofs are used in Simplified Payment Verification (SPV) in Bitcoin and in Stellar's state archival system. A client can verify a single transaction without downloading the full block.

puzzles.title: Full Cryptographic Pipeline
puzzles.description: Given a list of four transaction objects `[{from, to, amount}]`, build the Merkle root of their SHA-256 hashes, sign the root with an Ed25519 private key, and return a JSON object with `{root, signature, public_key}`.
hints: Serialize each transaction as a canonical JSON string: `JSON.stringify({from, to, amount})` with keys in alphabetical order.
Hash each serialized transaction with SHA-256 to get the leaf values.
Build the Merkle tree from those leaf hashes and extract the root.
Sign the raw bytes of the root hex string with Ed25519.
Return the root as hex, the signature as hex, and the public key as hex.
puzzles.explanation: This pipeline mirrors how blockchains bundle and authenticate transactions: individual TXs are hashed, combined into a Merkle tree, and the root is signed by the block producer. Verifiers can then independently recompute the root and verify the signature without replaying every transaction.
